s1.syndrome_frame: Subacute neurological deterioration with impaired extraocular movement, tetraparesis, and signs of meningeal irritation
salient_findings: Mild sinking of the right leg
key_facts: 10-year history of treatment with various medications
No history of severe lymphocytopenia
Impaired extraocular movement at last outpatient visit
Mild sinking of the right leg at position test
Developed dizziness and nausea a few months later
Received methylprednisolone treatment
Presented with moderate tetraparesis, headache, fever, and neck stiffness
Family members had fever, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea, recovering within 3 days
Patient had mild gastrointestinal symptoms prior to neurological symptoms
Positive Romberg test
Initial white blood cell count: 4900/μL
Lymphocyte count: 1240/μL
Later white blood cell count: 18,000/μL
Cerebrospinal fluid analysis showed increased protein level and 108 cells/mL
Cerebrospinal fluid culture was positive
MRI showed hyperintense lesion in the brainstem and cerebellum with slight contrast enhancement

shortlist.label: Listeria Meningitis
shortlist.why_kept: Positive cerebrospinal fluid culture and signs of meningeal irritation

shortlist.label: Cryptococcal Meningitis
shortlist.why_kept: Increased protein level in cerebrospinal fluid and impaired extraocular movement

shortlist.label: Tuberculous Meningitis
shortlist.why_kept: Subacute neurological deterioration and signs of meningeal irritation

shortlist.label: Brainstem Encephalitis
shortlist.why_kept: Hyperintense lesion in the brainstem and cerebellum on MRI

shortlist.label: Bickerstaff Brainstem Encephalitis
shortlist.why_kept: Impaired extraocular movement and mild sinking of the right leg

raw.rationale: The patient's symptoms, including impaired extraocular movement, mild sinking of the right leg, dizziness, nausea, and moderate tetraparesis, are consistent with brainstem involvement. The positive Romberg test and the presence of a hyperintense lesion in the brainstem and cerebellum on MRI also support this diagnosis. Additionally, the patient's symptoms and MRI findings are more consistent with an inflammatory or autoimmune process, such as Bickerstaff Brainstem Encephalitis, rather than an infectious process like meningitis.

rejected.why: The patient's symptoms and laboratory results, including the cerebrospinal fluid analysis, do not suggest a fungal infection like Cryptococcal Meningitis

rejected.label: Tuberculous Meningitis
rejected.why: The patient's symptoms and laboratory results, including the cerebrospinal fluid analysis, do not suggest a chronic infection like Tuberculous Meningitis

rejected.label: Brainstem Encephalitis
rejected.why: While the patient's symptoms are consistent with brainstem involvement, Bickerstaff Brainstem Encephalitis is a more specific diagnosis that is supported by the patient's symptoms and MRI findings
